account: RL-Math's weight change is 0.24 % of the weight norm with about 12 % of it in 8 input-output direction pairs per matrix; the input sides of those pairs are shared by on-policy RL on graded reasoning text (Code-RL 3.1 sits in them 5.2x more than Think-SFT, IF- and General-RL barely), are partly in place by step 100, and are new directions that the base's next layers read 1.4-1.7x more than random but only half as strongly as the base's own top directions.

Those pairs do two separable things, both carried by the 1.5x top-8 edit as long as each direction keeps its true input-output pair: they raise the share of samples that open in deliberation (Okay/Wait), and they lower the per-step slip rate along the whole derivation, which is why the edit votes level with RL on hard328 (216 vs 216, cued base 185) and wins 88 % of RL's per-sample lift on problems the cued base never solves.

An inference-time change can supply only the first part: the three-token cue, a plain answer that happens to open with Okay, or a one-tensor edit that writes the cue gives the base RL's opening, which is most of the MATH-500 gain (no cue 64, cue 82, RL 93: 18 of 29 points) once T 1.0 removes the repetition loops that hold about half of the long attempts at T 0.6.

Votes recover part of the second because the base's wrong answers are mostly one-off slips that scatter (same-problem wrong-pair agreement 0.26), so a vote of 4 adds about 7-11 points to the cued base against 3 for RL, but on hard328 the base has no right sample on 26 of the 36 problems RL's vote wins, so it stays at 195 against RL's 224 of 328.

The pairs are not a termination dial, a boxed-ending or format push, or a reward-specific output code: they change how a derivation continues, so they add right answers where the base already finishes, transfer to code mainly through opening and finishing, and their concentration in few directions comes from on-policy RL itself (an LM-judge reward concentrates as much, 0.127 vs 0.135), while the few slips left after them are shared, systematic wrong values.

Think-SFT, trained with no reward on long traces, writes a 100x larger diffuse change that still lies along the same input directions (4.8x chance), which is why a no-reward weight change matches or beats RL on hard328 (241 of 328) while no prompt, sampling setting or vote closes the last 9-11 points.

consequences.claim: How much more of Code-RL 3.1's change falls in Math-RL 3.1's top-8 input subspace than in General-RL 3.0's. S1 says the input sides are shared by RL on graded reasoning text (math, code) and not by LM-judge chat RL, so the ratio is far above 1 and far above what any reasoning-text change (Think-SFT) shows.
consequences.why_new: F51 and result-105d5c compare Code with Think-SFT inside Math 3.1's subspace. No fact or result compares the capture of one change by two different RL runs' subspaces (Math 3.1 vs General 3.0).
consequences.statistic: median over matrices of cap_right(code31>math31) / cap_right(code31>general30), a ratio
consequences.rows: all test matrices of the cap table (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down)
consequences.computation: For each test matrix compute r = cap['code31>math31']['cap_right'] / cap['code31>general30']['cap_right']. Statistic = median of r. 90 % interval: 2000 bootstrap resamples of matrices (with replacement), median each, 5th and 95th percentiles.
consequences.null: The same ratio for Think-SFT's change, cap_right(think_sft>math31)/cap_right(think_sft>general30) = 2.04 [1.92, 2.15] on explore, i.e. Math 3.1's input subspace takes any reasoning-text change ~2x better; chance subspaces give 1. Alternatives checked on explore: base-spectrum level cap_right(code31>general30)/cap_right(code31>base_w) = 1.08; Think-SFT math31/base_w ~1.5.

consequences.claim: Which matrices concentrate their change: the family-median-removed per-matrix top-8 share pattern of Math-RL 3.1 tracks Code-RL 3.1 much more than General-RL 3.0. S1/S5 say concentration in general comes from on-policy RL, but where it sits follows the shared reasoning pairs, which Code shares and the LM-judge run does not.
consequences.why_new: F24 compares Math 3.1 with IF and Think-SFT, and F62 compares Code with Think-SFT and IF. The Math 3.1-Code 3.1 vs Math 3.1-General 3.0 contrast is in no fact or result.
consequences.statistic: D = Spearman rho(Math31, Code31) - Spearman rho(Math31, General30) of family-median-removed top-8 shares, unitless
consequences.rows: all test matrices of the top8_share table
consequences.computation: On the test matrices, for each key k in {math31, code31, general30} take top8_share[k] minus the median of top8_share[k] over the test matrices of the same module. Compute Spearman rho between the math31 and code31 residuals and between the math31 and general30 residuals; D = difference. 90 % interval: 2000 bootstrap resamples of matrices (medians recomputed within each resample), 5th/95th percentiles.
consequences.null: D = 0 (General-RL concentrates in the same matrices as Code, as its equal overall top-8 share in F03 might suggest). Alternatives computed on explore: layer depth alone (product of each pattern's rho with layer) 0.057; base spectrum alone (via rho with base_w) -0.054; a common reasoning-text pattern routed through Think-SFT 0.24.

consequences.claim: How strongly the next layer of the base reads RL-Math's 8 written directions, relative to the base matrix's own top-8 directions. S1 says RL writes new pairs, not the base's dominant directions, which the base reads above random but at about half the gain of its own top directions.
consequences.why_new: result-ad95af reports the mean gain over random (1.67x). No fact states the per-writer ratio to the base's own top-8 directions, and no consequence has tested it.
consequences.statistic: median over writer matrices of rl.next / basew.next, a ratio
consequences.rows: all test writer matrices (o and down) of the xlisten table
consequences.computation: For each test writer row compute r = rl['next'] / basew['next']. Statistic = median of r. 90 % interval: 2000 bootstrap resamples of writer matrices, median each, 5th/95th percentiles.
consequences.null: RL amplifies the base's own dominant directions (as a dial on the base spectrum would), so the ratio is ~1. Alternative checked on explore: random directions give rand.next/basew.next = 0.35.

weights_cell.statistic: median over the 224 matrices of the share of RL-Math 3.1 step-100 change (squared Frobenius norm) inside Code-RL 3.1's top-8 input (right singular) subspace, a fraction
weights_cell.matrices: all 224 (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down of 32 layers)
weights_cell.computation: For each matrix: d_s = W(RL-Math 3.1 step 100) - W(base); d_c = W(RL-Code 3.1) - W(base); V_c = top-8 right singular vectors of d_c (truncated SVD); share = ||d_s V_c||_F^2 / ||d_s||_F^2. Report the median over 224 matrices.
weights_cell.why: S1: the input sides are shared across math and code RL and partly in place by step 100. Final Math-like changes sit in Code 3.1's input subspace at ~0.04, and the step-100 change carries ~0.66x the final concentration, which gives ~0.026. An account where step 100 is size-limited noise predicts chance (8/d_in, ~0.002) or the base-spectrum level (~0.009).
